title: Set the target first
principle: Test small first, and decide beforehand what result means yes.

screens.text: Let me tell you a story about idli batter. In 2006, PC Musthafa and his cousins started iD in Bengaluru with ₹50,000 and one small room. They put 100 packets into 20 stores. They gave themselves six months to reach their target.

screens.prompt: Of those first 100 packets, how many do you think came back unsold?
screens.why: About 90. Musthafa said 90 of every 100 packets used to come back, so they sold fewer than 10 a day. They were far from their target. After six months, they still had not reached it.

screens.prompt: Six months passed and they'd missed their target. What do you think they did next?

options.label: Kept the target and improved the batter
Lowered the target and called it a success
Rented a big factory to look serious

screens.why: Exactly. They did not lower the target or change the deadline. They kept working until they reached the target, three months late. Musthafa says getting the batter right took about nine months. Later, iD was in 1,000 stores across Bengaluru.

wrong.b: I see the thinking: lower the target, and now you have passed. But then the target cannot tell you if the idea worked. They kept their target and reached it three months late.
wrong.c: That means spending a lot before the idea has worked. With 90 of every 100 packets coming back, a factory would only make more unsold packets. They stayed small and fixed the batter first.

screens.title: Set the target first
screens.text: Decide what success means before you start the test. iD chose its target before it knew how sales would go. This is called pre-set success criteria: the number that means yes, and the date you will check it, written down first.

screens.prompt: Musthafa counted packets sold, not packets sent to stores. Why was that important?

options.label: Packets sent are easier to count
Anyone can send packets; only buyers decide sales

screens.why: Exactly. You can send 100 packets to stores whenever you want, but you cannot make shoppers buy them. Choose a yes number that only real customers can help you reach.

wrong.a: They are easier to count, but that does not prove customers want them. You could send 100 packets tomorrow and say you passed. Packets sold show what buyers actually chose.
wrong.b: Stores do not decide this. Packets sent go up when you send more. Packets sold only go up when customers buy them.

screens.title: Now try it with your idea
screens.text: iD started with a few stores before spending much more. You can do the same. Imagine you make homemade pickles and want to open a shop. Before renting a shop, you test your pickles at a Sunday market stall.

screens.prompt: The stall costs ₹6,000 a month. You earn ₹50 per jar. There are 4 Sundays. How many jars each Sunday pay for the stall?
screens.why: Well done. ₹6,000 ÷ ₹50 is 120 jars a month. 120 ÷ 4 Sundays is 30. So 30 jars only pays for the stall. Your yes number must be higher if you also want to earn money.

wrong.b: I see what you did: ₹6,000 ÷ ₹50 = 120. But that's for the whole month, and there are 4 Sundays, so it's 30 jars each Sunday.
wrong.c: Not quite. ₹6,000 ÷ ₹50 = 120 jars a month, and split over 4 Sundays, that's 30 jars each Sunday.

screens.prompt: Each jar leaves ₹50. Rent is ₹6,000 a month. You want ₹4,000 left after rent. What sales goal should you test?

options.label: Lots of people stop to taste
50 jars sold each Sunday by week 8

screens.why: Exactly. You need ₹6,000 for rent plus ₹4,000 left over. That is ₹10,000. At ₹50 a jar, that is 200 jars a month, or 50 each Sunday. Now you have a clear number and a date.

wrong.a: Tasting is free, so lots of people will do it. But your goal is ₹4,000 left after rent, and only paid jars get you there: 50 of them each Sunday.
wrong.c: You are right that it must be above 30. But how much above? Your ₹4,000 goal gives the answer: ₹10,000 ÷ ₹50 is 200 jars a month, or 50 each Sunday, by week 8.

screens.prompt: Your goal was 50 jars each Sunday by week 8. You sell 42. A friend says, "Open the shop anyway." What do you say?

options.label: Not yet. Change one thing and test again

screens.why: Exactly. At 42 jars, you make 42 × ₹50 × 4 = ₹8,400 a month. After rent, ₹2,400 is left. But you decided you need ₹4,000. Change one thing, such as the flavour or stall location, and test again, like iD fixed its batter.

wrong.a: I see why 42 feels close. But it leaves ₹2,400 after rent. Before the test, you decided the shop needs ₹4,000 left. Do not change that rule after seeing the result.
wrong.b: You decided on 50 before the test. Changing it to 42 after seeing the result would make the test unfair. Change one thing and test again.

screens.prompt: A shop costs ₹3 lakh to set up. The stall costs ₹6,000 a month for 2 months. What percent of ₹3 lakh is that?
screens.why: Exactly. 2 × ₹6,000 is ₹12,000. ₹12,000 out of ₹3,00,000 is 4%. So you spend ₹4 on the test for every ₹100 the shop would cost. A small test lets you learn before spending much more.

wrong.a: 40% would be ₹1,20,000. The test is only ₹12,000, which is 4% of ₹3 lakh.
wrong.c: 0.4% would be just ₹1,200. The test is ₹12,000, which is 4% of ₹3 lakh.

screens.prompt: I will show you six things you could do for your pickle business. For each one, choose: small test or big bet?

items.text: Sell a new lime flavour at one Sunday stall
Sign a 3-year lease on a shop
Buy 500 kg of limes for the new flavour
Supply one office canteen for a month
Print 5,000 labels with a shop address

screens.why: Exactly. A small test costs less and is easy to stop. A big bet uses much more money and is harder to stop. Test first. Spend more only after the test works.

screens.prompt: Put a good test in order.
steps: Write the yes number and the date
Run it, and count your numbers every Sunday
On that date, compare the result with the yes number
screens.why: Well done. You choose the yes number before the test. Then you count every Sunday. On the check date, compare the result with your number.

screens.text: Always, ___ you start a test, write down the ___ that means yes.
screens.why: Exactly. iD missed its date but did not change its target. It changed the batter instead. Pre-set success criteria help you judge the test by the result, not by what you hoped would happen.

summary: Start with a small, cheap version of the idea, and work out what result would make the big bet worth it.
Write that yes number and the date before you start, and count something buyers control.
If you miss, don't move the line. Change the offer and test again.

cards.front: Your pre-set success criteria said 12. The test hit 8. What now?
cards.back: Pre-set success criteria are set before the test for a reason. Change the offer, not the line.

cards.front: Stall rent ₹9,000 a month. Each sale leaves ₹30. Open 30 days. Sales a day to break even?
